questions.question: 1. In a singly linked list, can a node directly identify the node immediately before it?

answers.a: Yes, because every node stores a previous pointer
answers.b: No, because a standard singly linked-list node stores only its next link
answers.c: Yes, because memory addresses are always consecutive
answers.d: No, because singly linked lists contain no links

explanations.a: Incorrect. A previous pointer is not part of a standard singly linked-list node.
explanations.b: Correct. A standard singly linked-list node has a link to the next node but no direct link to its predecessor.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Linked-list nodes do not have to occupy consecutive memory locations.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Links are essential to connect nodes in a singly linked list.

questions.question: 2. Which field is normally present in a node of a singly linked list?

answers.a: Data and a link to the next node
answers.b: Data and links to both previous and next nodes
answers.d: Only the position of the node

explanations.a: Correct. A singly linked-list node normally contains data and a link to the next node.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The previous link is characteristic of a doubly linked list.
explanations.c: Incorrect. A node also needs to store the data represented by that node.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A position value is not the defining link information in a singly linked-list node.

questions.question: 3. What normally indicates the end of a non-circular singly linked list?

answers.a: The last node points to the first node
answers.b: The last node points to itself
answers.c: The last node's next link contains NULL
answers.d: The last node is stored at the largest memory address

explanations.a: Incorrect. Linking the last node to the first would make the list circular.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A self-link would create a cycle rather than mark the end of the list.
explanations.c: Correct. The absence of a next node is represented by a NULL next link.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Memory addresses do not determine which node is last in a linked list.

questions.question: 4. What is the worst-case time complexity of searching for a value in a singly linked list of $n$ nodes?

explanations.a: Incorrect. The desired value may be near the end of the list.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Sequential linked-list access does not support logarithmic search.
explanations.c: Correct. In the worst case, all $n$ nodes may be examined.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A single sequential search does not require quadratic work.

questions.question: 5. When inserting a node immediately after a known node in a singly linked list, how many existing nodes must be traversed to locate the insertion point?

answers.b: Only the known node is needed
answers.d: The number depends on whether the list is sorted

explanations.a: Incorrect. Traversal of all nodes is unnecessary when the insertion node is already known.
explanations.b: Correct. A direct pointer to the insertion node is sufficient to perform the local link updates.
explanations.c: Incorrect. There is no requirement to traverse half of the list.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Whether the list is sorted does not change the need for traversal when the target node is already referenced.

questions.question: 6. If `head` points to the first node and that node is deleted from a singly linked list, what must happen to `head`?

answers.a: It must point to the deleted node
answers.b: It must be set to the last node
answers.c: It must be updated to point to the former second node
answers.d: It must always be set to NULL

explanations.a: Incorrect. Keeping head at the deleted node would leave the list entry point referring to removed storage.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Deleting the first node does not require moving head directly to the last node.
explanations.c: Correct. The next node becomes the first node, so head must refer to that node.
explanations.d: Incorrect. NULL is appropriate only when there is no remaining node.

questions.question: 7. A singly linked list contains 10 → 20 → 30 → NULL. If `head` points to 10, what does `head->next->next->data` contain?

explanations.a: Incorrect. The starting node contains 10, before any `next` traversal.
explanations.b: Incorrect. One `next` traversal reaches the node containing 20.
explanations.c: Correct. Two `next` traversals reach the node containing 30.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The second `next` traversal reaches a valid node; NULL is reached after the next link from that node.

questions.question: 8. If a singly linked list contains $n$ nodes, what is the worst-case time complexity of deleting the last node when only the head pointer is available?

explanations.a: Incorrect. The predecessor of the last node may have to be found by traversal.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A singly linked list does not provide logarithmic access to its nodes.
explanations.c: Correct. Traversal may be required to locate the last node and its predecessor, giving $O(n)$ worst-case time.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Locating the last node requires at most one linear traversal, not quadratic work.

questions.question: 9. Which situation allows deletion of a node in a singly linked list to be performed without first traversing from the head to locate that node?

answers.a: The node itself is already directly referenced and the required neighboring information is available
answers.b: The list contains more than $n$ nodes
answers.c: The list is stored in contiguous memory
answers.d: The list is sorted in ascending order

explanations.a: Correct. A direct reference to the target, together with the information needed to reconnect the list, can avoid a search from the head.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The number of nodes does not by itself provide a direct reference to the target.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Linked-list deletion does not depend on contiguous storage.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Sorting does not by itself eliminate the need to locate the target and its predecessor.
